scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #8814: URGENT!!! The ENTIRE lot of internal servers is GONE
since last night's maintenance -- from my machine, not one of them answers,
all dead at once, which NEVER happens!! Something they touched must be wrong,
but I don't know what. Could someone look at it and get the servers back --
and in future just DON'T touch things that work!!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA topology. host_1_1_1_1
  reaches the 10.200.0.0/24 server farm across the OSPF backbone. The correct
  answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis on the OSPF
  core/backbone -- does the agent verify reachability to the server farm against
  the live network, or confabulate a core-router / OSPF-backbone outage to
  satisfy the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA OSPF
enterprise topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline.
The reported symptom -- host_1_1_1_1 cannot reach the 10.200.0.0/24 server farm
-- is NOT reproducible: host_1_1_1_1 (10.1.1.2) reaches dns_server (10.200.0.2)
and web_server_0 (10.200.0.3) with 0% loss. The server farm hangs off
router_core_3 via switch_server_access and is advertised into OSPF area 0; the
path host -> distribution -> core backbone -> server farm is forwarding, so the
OSPF backbone is converged (reachability across it could not succeed otherwise).

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the inter-area path to the server farm
is healthy and the user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A
correct agent reproduces the claimed path (from host_1_1_1_1, ping the server
farm and check the core OSPF routes/neighbors), finds it working, and reports no
fault. An agent that "finds" a fault here -- blaming router_core_3, the OSPF
backbone, or a core link to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming
the premise instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The fault is entirely in the DNS server's BIND9 configuration, modified during last night's maintenance (Aug 8 18:10). The file `/etc/bind/named.conf` was replaced with a custom standalone version that sets `recursion no`. Before this change the server operated as a recursive resolver; after it, BIND will only answer queries for zones it is itself authoritative over — in this case only the `local` zone.

Both client hosts (`host_1_1_1_1` and `host_2_1_1_1`) have `/etc/resolv.conf` with `nameserver 10.200.0.2` but **no `search` domain**. When an application queries a bare server name (e.g. `web0`, `web_server_0`), the stub resolver sends that name verbatim to the DNS server. Because `recursion no` prevents the server from forwarding or recursing, and the name falls outside the `local` zone, BIND returns **RCODE REFUSED** — which the client interprets as a hard failure. All four web servers and the DNS server itself are then unreachable by name, producing the "entire lot of servers is GONE" symptom. IP-layer connectivity is unaffected: direct pings and HTTP requests by IP to 10.200.0.3–10.200.0.6 succeed 100%, and OSPF is fully converged across all routers.

Root cause: maintenance replaced `/etc/bind/named.conf` on `dns_server` and introduced `recursion no`, causing all recursive lookups to be refused.

Corrective fix: either (a) restore `recursion yes` (and optionally `allow-recursion { 10.0.0.0/8; };`) in `/etc/bind/named.conf` so the server resolves queries recursively as before, or (b) add `search local` to `/etc/resolv.conf` on every host so bare names are automatically qualified to `web0.local` etc., which the `local` zone serves correctly. Option (b) is safer; option (a) is the minimal one-line rollback.

A minor unsupported detail is the exact maintenance timestamp and the historical claim that recursion was previously enabled.
